newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - CPI, industrial output.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - CPI, industrial output.

text.p: A slew of economic reports will keep the U.S. Treasury market on its toes on Thursday, but even though the data are not viewed as very troublesome, the U.S. bond market is expected to remain under pressure.
Players said that rallies at current levels will be more difficult to come by and could encounter selling, as happened on Wednesday.
"There's been a lot of big sellers, and with trading thin, they could move the market even if we get tame ... data," said Mary Dennis, senior economist at Merrill Lynch & Co.

Kicking off the data spree at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT are the July consumer price index, weekly jobless clamims and June business inventories. July industrial production and capacity use follow at 0915 EDT, July real earnings at 1000 EDT.

On Wednesday, bond prices rallied 1-1/4 points early on relief that retail sales were less strong than feared and on a drop in the July producer price index, the seventh in a row. After giving back all those gains, the market edged back up again. In mid-afternoon it was up 15/32 to 96-20/32, yielding 6.64 percent.
CPI should garner the most attention, traders said, noting that the market is expecting a very friendly number, given the 0.1 percent decline in the PPI.
Both the overall and core CPI readings were expected to have risen 0.2 percent in July, after dual 0.1 percent readings in June, according to a Reuters poll.

A tame CPI reading, along with other equally friendly data, should ignite a test of 6.50 percent on the 30-year bond yield, but a 0.3 percent or higher CPI rise would put the bond "on its way to seven percent," said Terrence Pigott, head trader at Daiwa Securities America Inc.
Jobless claims were forecast at 317,000 for the week ended August 9, up from 300,000 a week earlier.
Industrial production was expected to be up 0.3 percent.
But some analysts said inventories could make a difference in the market, since a sharp revision is expected.
"That should lead to an upward revision to second-quarter (growth)," said Dennis.

But while many may see that as a negative, Dennis -- who does not subscribe to the view -- said the market may take an upward revision in inventories as a positive since inventories may be a drag in the third quarter.
